title: Charity and disaster-relief fraud
body_md:
## Separate the cause, collector and destination
A disaster can be real while the payment link is false. An imitator may borrow a charity's name and photographs; a fundraiser may claim to collect for a named family without authorization; a legitimate crowdfunding organizer may still differ from the beneficiary. Emotional urgency is understandable, but it removes the time needed to trace the recipient. A dramatic picture or a friend's repost is not independent verification.

Start with the exact legal charity or named beneficiary. Find its site through a trusted prior reference or official registry and use the donation path it publishes. For crowdfunding, identify the organizer, beneficiary and platform's actual rules; if you cannot confirm that the organizer will pass funds on, choose a direct charity route. Registration requirements and tax treatment vary by country. The FTC's US guidance suggests checking state registration and, separately, IRS tax-exempt status where tax deductibility matters; a listing cannot prove every campaign honest.

Payment method matters too. The FTC warns that a fundraiser insisting on only cryptocurrency, gift cards, wires or payment apps is a strong danger signal in its US context. A genuine charity can offer many methods, including digital options; do not use one payment method as a universal authenticity test. HTTPS encrypts a donation form but does not establish its owner. Take a brief pause to verify; there is no universal 24-hour waiting requirement. Save the receipt and check whether you accidentally enabled recurring donations. If you paid a suspect fundraiser, promptly ask your payment provider about available options and report through the relevant local authority; reimbursement is uncertain.

blocks.title: A viral appeal with a changed wallet
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a widely shared post uses real flood photos and the name of an established aid group, but asks donors to send to a personal crypto wallet found only in the post.
blocks.analysis: Real photos and a real cause do not validate that wallet. Open the group’s official site independently and use its published donation channel. If the claimed campaign cannot be matched, do not send to the post.

blocks.title: A genuine urgent appeal
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a registered local relief group announces a same-day supply run. Its independently found site lists the project, exact legal entity, card donation form and a published contact; an organizer answers questions consistently.
blocks.analysis: Urgency alone does not make an appeal fraudulent. Confirm the entity and recipient under your country’s system, read the project and use the official payment route. You may donate promptly once satisfied; there is no magic waiting period.

blocks.title: Choose where the donation goes
blocks.setup: Synthetic: you want to help after a coastal storm. A friend forwards a moving social post linking to `coast-help.example`.

steps.prompt: The post names a known charity. How do you reach it?

choices.text: Find its official site or registry independently.
choices.consequence: You separate the charity from the forwarded URL.
choices.explanation: A genuine name can be used by an imitator.

choices.text: Click because your friend shared it.
choices.consequence: Your friend may have shared an unchecked link.

steps.prompt: The link is actually a crowdfunding page. What must be clear?

choices.text: Who organizes it, who receives it and how transfer to the cause is verified.
choices.consequence: You can decide whether this path serves the intended people.
choices.explanation: The organizer and beneficiary may be different.

choices.text: Only whether the photo is emotional.
choices.explanation: Emotion is not a transfer record.

steps.prompt: A caller says only gift cards will arrive in time. Next?

choices.text: Decline and use the independently verified donation route.
choices.consequence: You can support the cause without the forced payment method.
choices.explanation: A gift-card-only demand is a strong warning.

choices.text: Read gift-card codes over the phone.
choices.consequence: The codes may be spent immediately.

steps.prompt: After a legitimate donation, what follow-up catches a mistake?

choices.text: Save the receipt and inspect statement and recurring-payment setting.
choices.consequence: You can catch an amount or subscription you did not intend.
choices.explanation: FTC advises keeping records and checking what was charged.

choices.text: Delete the receipt because the charity is real.
choices.consequence: You lose a useful record if the charge differs.
choices.explanation: Legitimate payments can still need correction.

blocks.debrief: You can help quickly after tracing the legal recipient and payment path. A real crisis does not authenticate a particular post.

questions.prompt: A friend shares a photo of real damage with a wallet address. What does the photo prove?

choices.text: The event may be real; it does not link the wallet to aid.
choices.explanation: Content provenance and payment destination are separate.

choices.text: The wallet belongs to the victims.
choices.explanation: A photo cannot establish wallet ownership.

questions.prompt: A registered charity runs an urgent drive. Is waiting 24 hours mandatory?

choices.text: No; verify independently, then donate when ready.
choices.explanation: Verification, not a fixed delay, is the control.

choices.text: Yes; every urgent appeal is fraud until tomorrow.
choices.explanation: Genuine emergencies and honest rapid response exist.

questions.prompt: A US charity is on a tax-exempt list. What remains to check?

choices.text: That the particular campaign and payment destination are its own.
choices.explanation: Imitators can borrow a real charity’s name.

choices.text: Nothing; every link with its name is safe.
choices.explanation: A listing does not authenticate a social link.
